I'm not sure what the correct procedure for this is, but the IOG Plutus team would like to update the serialisation format for the Plutus Core  `array` type. 

## Plutus Core arrays
[CIP-0138](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/tree/master/CIP-0138) proposes the addition of a new array type to Plutus Core, together with new built-in functions  to operate on arrays.  The basic functionality was implemented in [PR #6727](https://github.com/IntersectMBO/plutus/pull/6727) in the `plutus` repository, with a number of later pull requests adding costing for the array operations, a specification, and a number of other things. 

## Serialisation and deserialisation
Plutus Core scripts are serialised using the [flat](https://hackage.haskell.org/package/flat) library, and this provides a serialisation method for arrays which was proposed as the serialisation method for Plutus Core arrays in the original version of CIP-0138.  However, [experiments](https://github.com/IntersectMBO/plutus/pull/7296#issue-3364894295) show that deserialisation times are noticeably quicker if `flat`'s list serialisation format is used instead and during deserialisation a list is read in and then converted to an array: this is faster because the list serialisation scheme is simpler than the scheme for arrays and the array deserialisation function involves initially constructing a list and then [converting that to an array](https://hackage.haskell.org/package/flat-0.6/docs/src/Flat.Instances.Array.html#decodeIArray) anyway.  We have also recently forked the `flat` library for use with Plutus Core and have [refactored the list decoder](https://github.com/IntersectMBO/plutus/pull/7358) to obtain further speed improvements.

In view of this we propose updating CIP-0138 to serialise Plutus Core arrays using `flat`s list serialisation scheme instead of its `array` serialisation scheme.

### Space versus time
`Flat`'s list serialisation scheme is slightly less space-efficient than its array serialisation scheme. The serialised elements of the list are separated by `1`-bits (with a `0`-bit at the end), whereas arrays are serialised in blocks of up to 255 elements with no separation between the serialised elements but with each block preceded by a single byte containing its length.  Thus serialising a 128-element array requires only one extra byte of overhead, but serialising a 128-element list requires 128 extra bits (16 bytes), but , an increase of 15 bytes over the array serialisation scheme (approximately 1/1000 of Cardano's current 16384-byte on-chain transaction size limit) .  However, rapid deserialisation is  important for the efficient functioning of the chain and we believe that the speed improvements arising from the use of the list decoder offest by the extra space.  Using a single encoding for both lists and arrays in Plutus Core also simplifies maintenance, specfication, and formalisation.

### Current implementation status
The Plutus Core array type and operations have all been fully implemented but are not expected to be enabled until the next hard fork, which is currently projected to happen in the early months of 2026.  Thus we can safely to change the serialisation method without affecting any existing scripts.  We have in fact [already updated](https://github.com/IntersectMBO/plutus/pull/7296) the array deserialiser to use our forked version of `flat`'s list serialisation scheme (although this could easily be reverted if necessary).  We would therefore like to update CIP-0138 to reflect this change and make it visible to the wider community in advance of the next hard fork.

Note that the process for opening a Plutus-related CIP no longer includes the requirement to specify a serialisation method (this was removed in #1038)

Note also that [CIP-0035](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/tree/master/CIP-0035#bug-fixes) states that a "fix may be submitted directly to the plutus repository and is NOT required to go through the CIP process." if "The specified behaviour is clearly wrong (in the judgement of relevant experts)"; we would claim that the change proposed in this PR meets these criteria.

The proposed change to signature checking is :

Currently, the `txid`, i.e. the hash of the transaction body, is signed. We propose this is changed to all keys instead signing the concatenation `txid ++ hash (required_observers)`.

The purpose of this change is to make the following light client project ([private repo](https://github.com/input-output-hk/innovation-cavefish)) faster, easier, and not dependent on sophisticated ZK techniques.

The purpose of this PR is to allow observer scripts to be treated as *intents*, which are, in some sense, separate from the transaction which has been constructed to satisfy them. Making the proposed change will allow for super-lightweight proof of intent fulfilment by a transaction, without ever having to inspect the contents of its fields except the `required_observers` field. 

The change:

Currently, the `txid`, i.e. the hash of the transaction body, is signed. We propose this is changed to all keys instead signing the hash of the concatenation `txid_and_obs = hash (txid ++ required_observers_hash)`. This would also require that the `TxBody` type contain the hash of the `required_observers` field *in addition* to the deserialized contents of the field, e.g. as a  separate field, or as a pair `(required_observers_hash , required_observers)`. Both `required_observers_hash` and `txid_and_obs` should be computed during transaction deserialization and included  in the deserialized `TxBody`.

This CPS is the result of [this](https://github.com/IntersectMBO/ouroboros-network/issues/4051) unintentional original design bug that used the "L" hash to settle ties, which gave a slight advantage to smaller pools.  After the Vasil hard fork, the network switched to using the "B" hash instead, which removed that advantage and led to some consternation amongst many smaller pool operators.

To address this, a PR was submitted that attempted to revert the change [here](https://github.com/IntersectMBO/ouroboros-consensus/pull/1548) with the primary objective of trying to stimulate the discussion amongst the relevant parties.  At the time it was unsure what the correct path should have been because the change from the L->B hash was not a CIP or a governance action, but a bugfix that might have flown under the radar of many of the SPOs it affected.

After discussion with @dcoutts it was decided that the proper path forward would be to write a CPS to properly define the problem first, since a technical solution to this would be more complex than simply reverting back from B->L hash, as the protocol was not intended to use the L hash for tiebreakers.

This CPS is the result of those discussions.  My hope is that it will stimulate some ideas for a future CIP that can hopefully allow us to solve the problem in a more permanent way.

Specify unValueData canonicality checks: require strictly ascending, distinct keys for both outer (currency symbols) and inner (token names) maps; fail on empty inner maps and zero-quantity entries; keep existing bounds/size constraints.

Add scaleValue builtin to the operation list: multiply all quantities by a provided integer, drop zeros / remove empty inner maps to preserve invariants, and fail on out-of-bounds results.

This allows `unValueData` to simultaneously serve two purposes, the first of which is to enforce that a `BuiltinData` is a canonical multi-asset value in data encoding, the second is to convert that `BuiltinData` to `BuiltinValue`. 

Importantly, this should allow the ex-unit cost of `unValueData` to be linear instead of quadratic.

This CIP proposes a specification for Ouroboros Tachýs: a variant of the Ouroboros protocol that uses a public slot leader schedule. Compared to Ouroboros Praos, Ouroboros Tachýs would achieve higher transaction throughput and lower transaction finality times. This protocol is not intended for use on the Cardano mainnet, but for use in Cardano-Cardano partner chains: that is partner chains to the Cardano mainnet that reuse Cardano implementations but with different Genesis and protocol parameters.

The advantage of this Ouroboros variant would be a higher block production rate: approximately 4 times higher compared to Ouroboros Praos. This leads directly to 4x higher TPS and substantially lower transaction finality times. Although the protocol is different, for tools and applications that use the blockchain it would remain highly compatible, allowing the reuse of existing and future Cardano tooling.

The main disadvantage of Tachýs compared to Praos would be not having the DDoS resistance that Praos provides. For partner chains intended to have relatively few block producers, the DDoS resistance Praos provides is of limited benefit. Other forms of DDoS resistance are required, and are possible.

For years we've had a list of practically random languages on the repository front page because — while all the deliberate content is Markdown — incidental content like shell scripts, diagnostic tools, profiling code, example code, etc. are the only files counted by [GitHub's analytics (via Linguist)](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/about-repository-languages) for that front page graphic.

What this currently says: our repository is over 50% Python and 30% Javascript + Typescript... which creates a false impression of both the content and purpose of the repository.  I think it's a shame that neither GitHub nor Linguist appear to support the classification of Markdown as a deliverable and consider it only incidental to "real" language content.

So I believe it's better not to have that language table showing at all: though the editors should be unanimous about this & anyone with a long-term interest in the repository should confirm it if possible: or suggest a better way of dealing with it than this hack (based on [this answer](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/34713765/github-changes-repository-to-the-wrong-language#answer-43520676)) that says (respectively for the 2 lines in `.gitattributes`):
1. Ignore files of all types in the repository.
2. Then look at & parse the Markdown files.

I would be happy to see Markdown included in the statistics: which it doesn't currently do, but maybe it will someday.  In the meantime we would finally be free of these "analytics" which tell the world that Cardano CIPs are written in Python & Javascript: which is a disruption both to Cardano learners and to ecosystem visitors, as well as an embarrassment to those more experienced.

I've tested this on my own fork and the Languages tab is removed immediately after reloading its front page: though it then gets reloaded (probably asynchronously) into the DOM from the upstream repository so it's there the next time the page is visited.  Therefore I expect that once this file is merged into `master` upstream then the table will finally be eradicated there.

##  Summary

  This CIP proposes adding a new optional block producer identification element to Cardano blocks in the Dijkstra era:

  Block Producer Identification: A free-form text field (1–32 bytes) wrapped in an extensible informational_data_set array added as the 6th element of the block body, allowing block
  producers to identify their node implementation and version, similar to HTTP user-agent strings.

##  Motivation

  With multiple node implementations entering block production (cardano-node, Amaru, Dingo, Torsten, Gerolamo), the ecosystem needs visibility into implementation diversity, upgrade
  progress, and network resilience through historical block analysis. Build metadata notation (e.g., +leios, +peras) enables tracking experimental feature deployment on testnets.

##  Key Features

  - 32-byte maximum matching Ethereum graffiti precedent
  - Block body placement — header remains unchanged
  - informational_data_set wrapper for future extensibility (additional fields can be appended without a new era boundary)
  - Minimum string length of 1 byte (nil already handles opt-out)
  - Optional (nil) preserving operator privacy
  - Purely informational — does not affect consensus
  - Implementation-agnostic specification via Cardano Blueprint

  *New Era Required*

  This proposal requires a new era as it modifies block CBOR serialization:

  - Block structure: 5 → 6 elements
  - Header: Unchanged
  - Block body hash computation includes new 6th element
  - Target era: Dijkstra

##  Technical Details
```cddl
  CDDL:
  block =
    [ header
    , transaction_bodies
    , transaction_witness_sets
    , auxiliary_data_set
    , invalid_transactions
    , informational_data_set / nil  ; NEW
    ]

  informational_data_set =
    [ producer_agent : tstr .size (1..32) / nil ]
```
##  Examples:
  - Mainnet: cardano-node/10.7.0
  - Testnet: amaru/1.1.0+peras
  - Privacy mode: nil

##  Links

  - [CIP-0180/README.md](https://github.com/disassembler/CIPs/blob/sl-ad/block-producer-id/CIP-0180/README.md)
  - Category: Ledger (per CIP-0084)
  - Status: Proposed

##  Authors

  - Samuel Leathers (@disassembler)
  - Adam Dean (@Crypto2099)

This CIP introduces **Optimistic Constitutionality**, changing how governance actions are approved under CIP-1694.

# Overview
Learning from the last nearly 100 Governance Actions onchain, no proposal that DReps wanted approved got rejected by the CC. The CCs effort however was insurmountable despite this perfect agreement. 

It turned out that DReps are excellent in filtering wrongful/bad proposals naturally by voting on their personal preference, regardless of constitutionality. This fact can be used to the network's advantage and reduce the cost of constitutional review drastically by borrowing from Zero Knowledge applications, where Optimistic Rollups (TRUE until someone says otherwise) is an effective expensive-verification-mitigation technique.

Optimistic Constitutionality shifts the CC from constant involvement to on-demand oversight, dramatically reducing workload and, among others, providing constructive aid to the ongoing debates around CC compensation.

# Changes proposed

Instead of requiring the Constitutional Committee (CC) to actively approve every action, proposals are assumed constitutional by default and move forward unless one CC member raises an objection by voting "No"/"Unconstitutional" - a "constitutional challenge" or veto. If such a challenge occurs, the original CIP-1694 approval process resumes, requiring full CC voting and the other CC members then either confirm the veto-ing CC's challenge by voting no/unconstitutional as well, or overrule it by voting yes/constitutional with the defined majority threshold. 

The required change is happening in the ledger logic for ratification, which is changed to: 

```math
$$\text{RATIFIED} \iff \left(V_{\text{CC}}^{\text{no}} = 0 \;\lor\; \frac{V_{\text{CC}}^{\text{yes}}}{|CC|} \geq T_{\text{CC}}\right) \wedge \left(\frac{S_{\text{DRep}}^{\text{yes}}}{S_{\text{DRep}}^{\text{active}}} \geq T_{\text{DRep}}\right) \wedge \left(\frac{S_{\text{SPO}}^{\text{yes}}}{S_{\text{SPO}}^{\text{delegated}}} \geq T_{\text{SPO}}\right)$$
```
`RATIFIED = (zero CC no votes exist **OR** (CC Yes votes ≥ CC threshold)) **AND** (DRep Yes stake ≥ DRep threshold) **AND** (SPO Yes stake ≥ SPO threshold)`

And, the introduction of a new  protocol parameter `ccOptimisticEnabled :: Bool` to control whether Optimistic Constitutionality is active or not, is helpful. 

# Path to Active 
This CIP requires additional code in the ledger, and can only be activated with a hardfork. Due to this, it will be beneficial to let the ecosystem vote on this via an info action, as this change will be packaged within a fork containing countless changes.  

> Possible Action NOW:
In order to not wait for the hard fork after the next hard fork to activate this and alleviate the CCs current pain, there is nice "soft activation" path forward, which could double as testing/confirmation period:
An info action, in which the CC announces it will from now insta-vote yes on everything by default without commentary, and only vote no once they are called or see issues themselves.

# RISKS
- **sleeping at the wheel**
Given that CC members are, and in fact must, be active community members, "sleeping at the wheel" risks are diminishingly low, as CC members (are assumed) to already follow Cardano Governance naturally anyway. This is additionally mitigated by now massively increased redundancy: Only 1 of (currently) 7 members must vote no. 

- **power abuse**
CC members could single-handedly block all approved, near-ratified Governance Actions by voting No/ calling out a "constitutional challenge" up until the last block of an epoch. This risk is real, and currently known possible mitigations for it, such as introducing approval window extensions are only increasing complexity a lot, introduce other issues, and overall provide no actual benefit. 
I postulate that the best mitigation for such power abuse would be to acknowledge the risk and rely on state of no confidence posteriori. 

# OPEN QUESTIONS
- I am not a ledger developer, so the currently contained suggested code changes under "Ledger Rule Changes" critically need to be reviewed. I used Opus 4.6 to generate them.

This PR introduces a new CIP for "Governance Action Addendums." Currently, proposers lack a standardized, on-chain mechanism to provide verifiable updates or clarifications to their active governance actions, leading to severe information asymmetry among voters (where only highly connected DReps receive off-chain context). 

This standard solves this by allowing authors to publish append-only, cryptographically verified updates using a dedicated transaction metadata label (1695) and an extension of the CIP-0100 JSON-LD schema. This ensures all voters have equal access to proposal refinements and rationale updates while strictly preserving the immutability of the original governance action.

Adds a draft CIP-100 extension defining three new JSON-LD document types (`DraftProposal`, `ProposalFeedback`, and `ProposalAddendum`, along with their relevant field definitions) for signed pre-submission drafts, signed public commentary, and binding author clarifications against governance proposals.

The intention is to provide richer on-chain bulletin board metadata around governance actions.

- Authors should be able to share early drafts in a community and tool agnostic way (i.e. solicit feedback from users regardless of whether they use twitter, the cardano forum, gov.tools, cexplorer, etc.) and without requiring the 100k deposit for an info action
- DReps and voters should be able to ask clarifying questions about a proposal, indicating what clarity it would take to change their vote, etc.
- Proposal authors should be able to correct typos, clarify ambiguous language, and address concerns in a *restricting and socially-binding* way

The above signal can feed into our off-chain enforcement processes like the intersect budget process. It gives clearer mandates for those tasked with interpreting the will of the DReps when the messy nature of the real world inserts itself into our clean ivory-tower notions of "just do what the DReps voted for", and allows strategic flexibility.

Note that CIP-100 doesn't actually require me to standardize this; I could just publish the context document somewhere and ask tooling authors to begin adopting it if it's useful and popular.

However, since I'm hoping this *will* become standard, I'm opening the CIP early, to give it a canonical URL in the context and avoid the URL changing in the future.

# Cardano Wallet Deep-Link Signing

([rendered latest document](https://github.com/Flux-Point-Studios/CIPs/blob/feat/cip-deeplink-signing-draft/CIP-0186/README.md))

## Summary

This CIP defines a deep-link wire protocol that lets a native mobile dApp ask an installed Cardano wallet to perform CIP-30 operations (chiefly `signTx` and `signData`) over the OS's URL-handling mechanism — no relay server, no embedded WebView, no QR, no WebSocket. It closes the gap CIP-30's `window.cardano` injection contract cannot reach: mobile-native dApps running outside a wallet-controlled browser context.

## Solution-To: CPS-0010

[CPS-0010 (Wallet Connectors)](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/tree/master/CPS-0010) documents that CIP-30 is a JavaScript-injection contract over a shared browser `window` object, and explicitly enumerates "mobile-native dApps" as an unaddressed connector shape. This proposal addresses that gap by specifying a transport profile for CIP-30's existing method surface — `signTx`, `signData`, `getUsedAddresses`, `getRewardAddresses`, `getNetworkId`, with optional `submitTx` and a reserved CIP-95 `signGovernance` profile — over OS deep-links (Universal Links on iOS, App Links on Android), with an X25519-encrypted payload and a BLAKE2b-256 commit binding so the wallet can prove which transaction it actually signed. The CIP does not replace CIP-30; a wallet that implements both serves browser-extension, in-app WebView, and mobile-native dApps with one signing engine.

## Reference Implementations

Two reference implementations are in active development under Flux Point Studios, alongside a companion repo for context:

- **[`cip30-deeplink-client`](https://github.com/Flux-Point-Studios/cip30-deeplink-client)** — dApp-side TypeScript SDK (Apache-2.0). Public repository created at draft submission; README and anticipated public surface are published, with source landing in Wave 2. The SDK is consumed by the Aegis iOS app (Aegis itself is closed-source; only the on-chain validator suite is public — see below).
- **[`yuti`](https://github.com/Flux-Point-Studios/yuti)** — wallet-side reference implementation (Flutter, iOS + Android + PWA, Apache-2.0). Yuti will implement the URL handler in Swift (iOS) and Kotlin (Android), plus a `lib/services/cip30_deeplink_service.dart` adapter that decrypts the payload and routes to Yuti's signing engine. The receiver patch is estimated at ~290 lines across 8 files; this is the patch surface we propose Lace / Eternl / Vespr / Typhon / Yoroi / SecondFi could adapt against their existing signing engines.
- **[`aegis-contracts`](https://github.com/Flux-Point-Studios/aegis-contracts)** — companion repo only (not part of this CIP). The on-chain Aiken validator suite for Aegis, V12.2 live on Cardano preprod. Listed for completeness so reviewers can see the production context the dApp-side SDK is consumed from. The CIP itself is a wallet/dApp transport, with no on-chain surface.

Reference implementation status (transparent — both impls are pre-shipping at the time of this PR open):

- dApp-side SDK (`cip30-deeplink-client`): repo public, README populated; source targeted for the next Aegis mobile wave (4-6 weeks).
- Yuti receiver: repo public, license + security policy + CIP cross-references in place; receiver patch targeted in parallel (4-6 weeks for receiver, +2-4 weeks for signing-engine integration).
- First end-to-end `signTx` round trip on preprod: targeted within 8-12 weeks of this PR opening.

These dates are well inside the 6-month median Cardano-Foundation review window for new CIPs, so the spec will have empirical preprod evidence by the time editors are ready to merge. We chose to open the Draft PR early to surface the design to editors and other wallet teams as soon as possible, not to claim premature implementation.

## Prior art surveyed

- **EIP-831 (Ethereum) — URI envelopes**: <https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-831>. One-way URIs only; no encryption, no callback. Useful as a URI-syntax precedent.
- **Solana MWA 2.0 (Mobile Wallet Adapter)**: <https://github.com/solana-mobile/mobile-wallet-adapter>. Uses P-256 ECDH + WebSocket + reflector. Optimised for high-throughput in-app gaming (Saga phone); their 2024 retrospective recommended Safari Web Extensions for low-throughput dApps — which is exactly the shape this CIP targets, with the Phantom/Petra deep-link pattern instead.
- **Phantom Deep-Links (Solana)**: <https://docs.phantom.com/phantom-deeplinks/provider-methods>. Universal Links plus NaCl box (X25519 + XSalsa20-Poly1305). Mainnet evidence across years of production. The encryption envelope and `dappKey`/`walletKey`/`nonce`/`payload` URL shape proposed here mirrors theirs.
- **Petra Deep-Links (Aptos)**: <https://petra.app/docs/deep-link-api>. Same construction as Phantom, custom-scheme transport. Confirms the design generalises beyond Solana.
- **BIP-21 (Bitcoin URIs)**: <https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0021.mediawiki>. Bare-URI payment intents, no signing roundtrip — included as a "what NOT to do" precedent for signing flows.
- **CIP-45 (Cardano WebRTC)**: <https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/tree/master/CIP-0045>. The closest existing Cardano connector for mobile, but assumes a WebTorrent tracker as relay. This CIP is complementary — WebRTC remains the right answer for desktop-browser-to-mobile-wallet; deep-link is the right answer for mobile-to-mobile on one device.
- **CIP-0162 (Cardano URIs - DRep Links)**: <https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/tree/master/CIP-0162>. Recently merged. Establishes precedent for the `web+cardano` URI family. This CIP intentionally does NOT use that family because the deep-link target is a wallet vendor's Universal Link domain (`https://lace.io/...`), not a Cardano-namespace URI.

## Open questions for reviewers

1. **`submitTx` MUST vs MAY?** The current draft marks `submitTx` as OPTIONAL on the wallet side because dApps with their own submission backend (the Aegis case) do not need it. Should we instead require it so dApps without infrastructure can rely on the wallet? Tradeoff: required `submitTx` adds an attack surface (wallet now relays arbitrary signed tx) but eases dApp authors.

2. **CIP-95 governance in v1 or v1.1?** The draft reserves the method name `signGovernance` and references the CIP-95 surface, but does not fully specify the URL envelope for vote delegations, DRep registrations, or governance proposal data signatures. Should v1 cover these too, or is a follow-up profile (v1.1) once CIP-95 itself reaches Active the right call? Editor preference here would help us scope.

3. **URL length budget — 12 KB the right ceiling?** The draft mandates wallets accept URLs up to 12 KB and MAY refuse larger. A typical Aegis insurance buy CBOR is 1.2-3 KB pre-encoding; multi-asset txns can push 6 KB. iOS Safari and Android Chrome both handle 32 KB, but Universal Link previews truncate around 8 KB. Is 12 KB the right pragmatic ceiling, or should the spec mandate 16 KB / 24 KB to accommodate complex Plutus transactions? (We can pre-publish reference scripts via CIP-31 to shrink, but smaller dApps may not.)

4. **Wallet registry — central vs decentralised?** Appendix B of the draft proposes a central `wallet-registry.json` maintained in this CIP's folder, listing each wallet's `id`, `scheme`, and `https` prefix. An alternative is to require each wallet to publish its own `apple-app-site-association` / `assetlinks.json` at a CIP-defined well-known path and have dApps probe at runtime. The central registry is faster to iterate but adds CIP-editor maintenance burden. Editor preference?

5. **iOS custom-scheme fallback — keep or drop?** The draft retains `cip30dl:` as a fallback for the install-but-no-AASA-yet edge case. Custom schemes have a well-documented hijacking risk (any app can register the scheme after install). The fallback is rate-limited by the `redirect` host binding, but a strict-Universal-Links-only profile is also viable. We lean keep-as-defence-in-depth; reviewers may disagree.

## Test plan

The spec will be validated empirically by the two reference implementations end-to-end. Test cases (all to be exercised on Cardano preprod before any Active-status push):

- **Aegis ↔ Yuti happy path** (`connect` → `signTx` → `getUsedAddresses` → `disconnect`) — to be captured in a published Aegis ↔ Yuti integration test once both impls land.
- **Replay rejection** — same `(dappKey, nonce)` tuple is replayed inside `ttl + 600s`; wallet MUST return `errorCode -5 NonceReplay`.
- **Commit-mismatch rejection** — dApp builds CBOR, wallet receives a different CBOR with the original `commit` URL parameter; wallet MUST return `errorCode -2 CommitMismatch` BEFORE rendering signing UI.
- **Redirect host-binding rejection** — second app re-uses captured `session` token with a different `redirect` host; wallet MUST return `errorCode -4 RedirectHostMismatch`.
- **TTL-expired rejection** — `ttl < now`; wallet MUST return `errorCode -6 TtlExpired`.
- **Conformance suite** — to be published under `cardano-foundation/cip-deeplink-conformance` once draft merges. Suite is the Aegis ↔ Yuti integration harness, generalised to drive any wallet under test.

Target Path-to-Active metrics, repeated from the CIP body:
- 1 production wallet ships on iOS App Store + Google Play.
- 1 production dApp ships a mobile-native client with ≥ 1,000 mainnet transactions signed via this protocol over a 30-day window.
- Conformance suite published and passed by all implementing wallets.
- A second wallet interoperates with the same dApp without dApp-side code changes.

## Co-author opportunity

The draft is intentionally aligned with the Phantom / Petra protocol shape so the wallet-side patch surface inside an existing signing engine is small (~400 lines around a URL handler). We explicitly invite the **Lace, Eternl, Vespr, Typhon, and Nami** teams to be listed as co-authors in v1.1 once they review the spec and confirm the patch surface is workable inside their codebases. Discussions are open at `contact@fluxpointstudios.com` and on this PR thread. Our goal is to ship v1.1 with all five wallets as named co-authors and at least two of them as named Implementors in the preamble.

## Out-of-band

- The Aegis team will summarise this draft at the next CIP editors' biweekly meeting (HackMD agenda link to be added once the meeting page is open).
- Cardano Forum thread for pre-PR discussion (already open): <https://forum.cardano.org/t/cip-proposal-mobile-deep-link-signing-for-native-dapps-cip-30-extension/154561>. The same URL is set on the CIP's `Discussions:` front-matter field.
- Reference impl repos and the conformance suite repo will move from `Flux-Point-Studios/*` to a vendor-neutral home under `cardano-foundation` if editors prefer; today they live where the maintainers do.

Thank you for your time on review.

## Summary

This PR proposes a new CIP: **Utilization-Scaled Pledge Bonus**.

The Cardano reward formula's pledge bonus `A = r · a₀ · P / (1 + a₀)` depends on operator pledge `P` but not on pool total stake `S`. As `S` grows, the per-delegator share `(A − F)/S` strictly falls — adding delegation to a high-pledge pool dilutes everyone already there. This punishes the rational-delegator behavior the protocol's Nash equilibrium assumes.

The proposal multiplies the pledge bonus by pool utilization `u = min(S, S_sat) / S_sat`:

```
A_new = r · a₀ · P · min(S, S_sat) / (S_sat · (1 + a₀))
```

A saturated pool earns exactly today's bonus. A half-utilized pool earns half. An empty pledged pool earns nothing until delegators arrive. **No new parameter is introduced** — `a₀` retains its name, governance dial, and Sybil-resistance role. Sybil resistance is in fact strengthened at the formula level: splitting an MPO's pledge across N pools reduces total bonus by roughly 1/N.

This PR proposes replacing the **wFA^LS (weighted Fait Accompli with Local Sortition)** voting-committee scheme currently specified in CIP-164 with a simpler **stake-based committee** scheme. The committee for an epoch is fixed at the epoch boundary by ordering pools by stake (descending) and selecting them, in order, until a configured cumulative-stake target is met. There are no per-EB elections, no non-persistent voters, and no per-vote sortition proofs. Every committee member is eligible to vote on every EB within the epoch.

The motivation is **certificate size and verification cost on the critical path**. Under wFA^LS, the bulk of certificate size and verification cost comes from the non-persistent voters' eligibility proofs. Removing local sortition eliminates that overhead. The certificate collapses to a bitfield over a known committee plus a single aggregated BLS signature. The following comparison uses the [`leios-wfa-ls-demo`](https://github.com/cardano-scaling/leios-wfa-ls-demo) benchmarks against mainnet stake data, with the wFA^LS configuration of 481 PVs + 94 NPVs as the reference point:

|                                       | wFA^LS (current spec)   | Stake-based, equivalent coverage (this PR) |
| ------------------------------------- | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Committee size                        | 481 PV + 94 NPV         | 916 voters (top-stake at 99% cumulative, mainnet epoch 612) |
| Certificate size                      | ~6.8 kB                 | ~203 bytes (bitfield ⌈916/8⌉ + agg. sig. + overhead) |
| Certificate verification (worst case) | ~10 ms                  | ~2 ms                                      |
| Vote size                             | 94 B (PV) / 171 B (NPV) | 94 B (uniform)                             |
| Vote verification                     | 427 μs / 1750 μs        | 427 μs (uniform)                           |

**On equivalent coverage.** Mainnet has roughly 3,000 SPOs with a Gini coefficient of ~0.84. Stake distribution data across 51 recent epochs (562–612, summarized in [Paul Clark's stake-distribution analysis](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1CmSC8BRDZTH32fk_bZ4db6baYGodZMB-71b-S18B2PQ)) shows highly stable coverage thresholds:

| Cumulative stake | Pools required (epoch 612) | Range across epochs 562–612 |
| ---------------- | -------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| 90%              | 471                        | 471–503                     |
| 95%              | 601                        | 601–636                     |
| 99%              | 916                        | 911–956                     |

The trend is gently *decreasing* (consolidation toward larger pools), which tightens the argument over time rather than weakening it. wFA^LS's configuration of 481 PVs + 94 NPVs gives expected coverage near 100% per round, but only as a *sample* of the residual — NPVs are stake-weighted Poisson draws, not a census. **Stake-based truncation at 99% cumulative coverage (916 voters at epoch 612) therefore matches wFA^LS's effective security regime closely**: both schemes capture the dominant top-471 (the 90% cut, essentially the same set as the 481 PVs), and the 99% cut additionally captures most of the same tail that wFA^LS's NPV draws sample from. The remaining ~1% of stake — fragmented across ~2,000 very small pools with a long Pareto tail — is too dispersed to threaten the 75% quorum under any of the schemes. Doubling the committee from ~480 (90% cut) to ~916 (99% cut) increases certificate size only by the bitfield delta of ~55 bytes; the cert-size argument is essentially invariant across the 90%–99% coverage range. The size estimate above (~203 B) is back-of-the-envelope and will be replaced with a measured value from the wfa-ls-demo before merge.

Certificates are perpetual on-chain overhead; certificate verification is on the critical path between receiving a certifying RB and being ready to extend the chain; votes diffuse under a tight $L_{\text{vote}}$ budget. The reductions compound: at coverage parity with wFA^LS, the cert-size reduction is over an order of magnitude (~6.8 kB → ~203 B, ~33×) and certificate verification time drops ~5×.

### Scope

The change is a refinement of the certificate format and committee-selection rules, not a redesign. CIP-164 Appendix A already states that *"alternative schemes satisfying these requirements could be substituted"*; this PR exercises that explicit extension point.

**Unchanged:**

- BLS over BLS12-381
- The 75% quorum value
- Certificate inclusion timing constraints
- The LeiosNotify / LeiosFetch mini-protocols
- The threat model

**Changed:**

- **Committee structure** — dual PV/NPV → single stake-truncated set
- **Vote structure** — two shapes → one uniform shape
- **Certificate format** — per-NPV eligibility proofs → bitfield + single aggregated signature
- **Epoch-boundary computation** — Fait Accompli precomputation → stake-ordered truncation
- **Quorum definition** — head-count fraction of committee → minimum fraction of total active stake
- **Appendix A requirements** — updated to reflect public deterministic committee, key rotation as a should-have, and loosened liveness bound

**Explicitly out of scope:**

- **BLS key rotation mechanism.** The adaptive-security claim applies equally to *all three* schemes considered (All-vote, stake-based truncation, wFA^LS) only under the assumption of regular rotation; without rotation, the static-vs-adaptive distinction collapses regardless of committee scheme. The on-chain mechanism (pool registration certificate path, epoch-boundary activation, prevention of within-epoch grinding) is a meaningful spec change in its own right and is left to a follow-up PR amending this CIP.
- **VRF key rotation.** Related, but Praos-layer and outside CIP-164.
- **A fixed committee size.** The parameter is a cumulative-stake target (or maximum-error equivalent); realized committee size tracks the stake distribution.

### Evidence

1. **[`cardano-scaling/leios-wfa-ls-demo`](https://github.com/cardano-scaling/leios-wfa-ls-demo)** — Haskell implementation of wFA^LS on mainnet stake data, with the vote/cert size and verification benchmarks cited above.
2. **[ARC voting crypto review](https://github.com/input-output-hk/ouroboros-leios/blob/41cefc99a/docs/arc-voting-crypto-review.pdf)** — cryptographic analysis comparing All-vote, Truncation (the scheme in this PR), and wFA^LS on adaptive-security and overhead grounds. With BLS key rotation, all three schemes provide comparable adaptive security in the practically-relevant regime; the one feature wFA^LS uniquely retains is non-targetability of non-persistent voters, but the persistent voters under wFA^LS are precisely the largest pools an adaptive attacker would already target. Also provides formal pen-and-paper algorithms for the voting and certificate scheme.
3. **[Network simulations](https://github.com/input-output-hk/ouroboros-leios/tree/main/analysis/sims/2026w18)** — results on `mini-mainnet` (750 nodes) and a derived `midi-mainnet` (1,500 nodes) show throughput, EB certification rate, and below-threshold rates essentially identical across the three schemes at all tested loads (0.150–0.350 TxMB/s), and stake-based truncation within the $L_{\text{vote}}$ budget. To stress committee size directly on the same topologies, an "everyone votes" mode was also simulated — literally every node including relays, yielding committee sizes of 750 and 1,500 respectively — and the protocol still performed as expected. The signal so far is that committee size does not dominate performance at these scales, which significantly reduces (but does not fully eliminate) the concern that vote diffusion could be a limiting factor. **Caveat:** these runs are on topologies smaller than full mainnet (~3,000 SPOs); the `midi-mainnet` is similarly connected to mainnet but not the same scale, so a full-scale mainnet-equivalent run remains outstanding. On current evidence, the wFA^IID variant is retained in the CIP's [Design Decisions](CIP-0164/README.md#voting-committee-selection) as a forward-looking option rather than a fallback the data calls for; rationale and remaining caveats are recorded there.

### To be discussed

1. **Naming.** Is "stake-based committee" the right name? Internal discussion has used "Truncate", "top-stake-fraction", and "stake-based cutoff" interchangeably. Proposal: **stake-based committee** as the formal spec name, with **stake truncation** as an acceptable synonym informally.
2. **Parameter shape.** *Cumulative stake covered* (e.g. 99%) vs *maximum truncation error* (e.g. ≤1%). The two are equivalent. Slight preference for the error formulation because the same parameter shape generalizes across all three schemes — useful for the staged-fallback story in *Alternatives & Extensions* — but cumulative-stake is more intuitive.
3. **Quorum as a stake threshold.** The current spec defines $\tau$ as a "minimum fraction of committee votes required for certification" — a head-count fraction over committee members. This PR redefines $\tau$ as a **minimum fraction of total active stake** whose votes must be present in the certificate. $\tau = 0.75$ means exactly "votes from pools holding ≥75% of total active stake have signed." The security argument (certified EBs are known to >25% of honest stake even under 50% adversarial stake) is then stated directly in terms of stake, not voter count. Under head-count quorum, a coalition of many small committee members could satisfy the threshold while representing far less stake than a smaller set of large pools — the quorum would not measure what the security property actually requires. With a stake threshold, the certificate directly proves the predicate the diffusion-period safety argument relies on. This also gives a natural constraint between the two parameters: $\sigma_c > \tau$, i.e. the committee must cover more stake than the quorum demands, or certification is impossible. At $\sigma_c = 0.99$ and $\tau = 0.75$ there is a 24-percentage-point margin between what the committee covers and what the quorum requires.

## Summary

Token-Owned Addresses (TOA) define a deterministic Cardano enterprise script address for a controlling asset class `(policy_id, asset_name)`. The address is the hash of a canonical Plutus V3 validator applied to `(toa_version, policy_id, asset_name)`, spendable by any transaction that consumes exactly one unit of the controlling NFT as input, produces exactly one unit as output, and does not mint or burn that asset class in the same transaction.

This is an off-chain interoperability CIP — no ledger changes are required. Conformance is determined by the compiled un-applied validator artifact, the canonical parameter encoding (CDDL), the address-derivation procedure, validator rules, and normative test vectors.

Status: `Proposed`.

## Related work

- **Builds on:** CIP-0014 (asset fingerprint), CIP-0019 (addresses), CIP-0067 / CIP-0068 (asset name labels and datum metadata), CIP-0069 (Plutus script type uniformization).
- **Complementary:** CIP-0143 (Inactive) and CPS-0003 share the deterministic-derived-script-address pattern applied to programmable transfer behaviour for fungible tokens; TOA applies it to NFT-controlled vault addresses.
- **Forward-compatible with:** CIP-0160 for future deposit-restriction extensions.
- **External prior art:** ERC-6551 (Ethereum Token-Bound Accounts), Solana Associated Token Accounts.

## Reference implementation and demo

Published at [en7angled/toa@0.1.0](https://github.com/en7angled/toa/releases/tag/0.1.0):

- Plinth validator + compiled un-applied UPLC artifact (476 bytes, template hash `129181a58ca3716aada61244d3d4210bff5a7235f709189af2596dc0`, artifact blake2b-256 `7f78c5524a00852eb51ee760f86a3f0cce4535b446e0c03d6cdc35eb6de0092b`).
- Six normative address-derivation test vectors covering ASCII / empty / max-length / CIP-67 label 100 / CIP-67 label 222 / `toa_version` isolation.
- Atlas-based off-chain library + Servant HTTP API + Swagger UI.

Demo: [toa.e7d.tech](https://toa.e7d.tech) — runs the reference frontend against Cardano Preview and mainnet, exercising address derivation, deposit, spend, and NFT carry-through end-to-end.

## Path to Active

7 of 9 acceptance criteria are satisfied by the reference implementation. Outstanding work is community-owned:

- Validator-scenario test vectors + verification by an independent implementation on a different stack (lucid-evolution, MeshJS, cardano-transaction-lib, PyCardano, or similar).
- Wallet and explorer/indexer integrations labelling TOA addresses and surfacing the policy classification.

This PR proposes a new Cardano Problem Statement (CPS-????) addressing the lack of vote privacy for Delegated Representatives (DReps) under CIP-1694.

All DRep votes are currently recorded in plaintext on the public ledger the moment the voting transaction is confirmed. While transparency supports accountability, unrestricted real-time visibility creates concrete problems: vote-buying, coercion during the voting window, herding toward the apparent majority, cartel signalling among large DReps, and a chilling effect on minority positions.

## Summary

Adds a normative section to CIP-0057 that specifies how parametric (generic) type instantiations are named in the `definitions` registry, how `$ref` strings target them under RFC 6901, and how `title` is to be populated.

The amendment is **purely additive** — no existing fields, keywords, or examples are changed. The new section codifies a single angle-bracket syntax for generic instantiations and acknowledges an earlier dollar-separator form as legacy that new producers MUST NOT emit and consumers MAY (but need not) accept.

The text is written so that a future reader of the CIP will read the parametric-types section as part of the original specification — no "earlier revisions", "we chose", or amendment-narrative voice in the CIP body itself. Specific producers are also not named in the normative or rationale sections.

### What the section specifies

**Interop-critical (MUST):**

- **Definition keys**: angle-bracket grammar — `Option<Int>`, `List<ByteArray>`, `Pair<Int,ByteArray>`, `Map<K,V>`, nested arbitrarily (`List<Option<types/order/Action>>`). Module separators stay as forward slashes inside the qualified name.
- **Tuples**: doubled angle brackets — `Tuple<<A,B>>`, `Tuple<<A,B,C>>` — to disambiguate from a hypothetical single-argument generic `Tuple<A>`.
- **`$ref` escaping**: standard JSON Pointer (RFC 6901) — `/` → `~1`, `~` → `~0`, angle brackets and commas pass through verbatim.
- **Type identity** for parametric instantiations is carried by the definition key / `$ref`; consumers MUST NOT use `title` to distinguish entries.

**Hint, not interop-load (SHOULD / MAY):**

- **`title`** SHOULD hold only the bare constructor name (`"Option"`, not `"Option<Int>"`) so it works directly as a code-generation hint, but producers MAY emit the parameterized form. Consumers MUST tolerate either form; if they derive identifiers from `title`, they strip the angle-bracket suffix.

### Legacy syntax handling

- **New producers MUST NOT** emit the dollar-separator form (`Option$Int`, `List$ByteArray`) or any other historical separator.
- **Consumers MAY support** legacy forms for backwards compatibility with older blueprints, but are NOT required to. A consumer that rejects legacy-form blueprints outright is still conformant with this spec.
- When a legacy-supporting consumer produces keys itself (e.g. synthesised auxiliary definitions during code generation), it MUST emit the modern angle-bracket form regardless of what it consumed.

### What this amendment intentionally does NOT do

- It does not deprecate or remove anything that existing tools depend on. Existing blueprints remain valid; only new producers are constrained on the MUST rules.

## Motivation (PR-side; not in the CIP text)

Today CIP-57 is silent on parametric-type naming. As blueprints have appeared from a widening set of producers, conventions diverged for separating a type constructor from its arguments (`Option$Int`, `Option<Int>`, and bespoke separators in between). Without a normative rule, every new producer is free to invent a third or fourth.

Concretely: Bloxbean's cardano-client-lib annotation processor has carried dual `<>` / `$` parsing for two years because it has to consume both. We're cleaning that out on the library side now and this PR is the upstream half of that work — pinning the convention so future producers don't reintroduce the divergence. SHOULD wouldn't actually prevent that for definition keys / `$ref` / encoding, so those rules are MUST. `title`, by contrast, doesn't carry type identity (consumers reach identity through the key), so a MUST there would constrain producers without unlocking interop and is SHOULD instead.

## Findings from real-world verification

The first draft of this amendment put a MUST on `title` requiring the unparameterized form. After authoring a batch of integration tests that compile real Aiken stdlib v3.1 contracts and feed them through code generation, I observed that one blueprint emits **both** forms in `title`:

- `Option<X>` → title `"Option"` (unparameterized — matches the rule)
- `Tuple<<A,B>>` → title `"Tuple"` (unparameterized)
- `Pairs<A,B>` → title `"Pairs<A, B>"` (parameterized)

A MUST that says "title is the unparameterized name only" would therefore declare real Aiken output non-conformant for one specific type while adding no interop benefit. Identity flows through the definition key and `$ref`, both of which remain MUST and unambiguous. This is why the title rule is SHOULD with explicit consumer-side tolerance for the parameterized form.

## Rationale (also expanded inline in the CIP)

- **Familiarity**: angle brackets are the dominant generics syntax in target languages (Java, TypeScript, Rust, C#, Scala). Code generators can use the key string nearly verbatim.
- **Compositionality**: nesting is unambiguous (`List<Option<Foo>>`); identifier-character separators collide with target-language identifiers and need extra escaping for nesting.
- **Ecosystem alignment**: current major producers already emit the angle-bracket form. Standardising on what new producers already emit minimises churn.

JSON Pointer's `~1` escape is reused rather than introducing a new mechanism, because RFC 6901 is already the substrate `$ref` is built on.

## Versioning / change-tracking

CIP-1 § Versioning treats CIP-text revisions as git-history-tracked rather than version-tagged ("this does not apply to the CIP text, for which annotated change logs are automatically generated... as a history of CIP files and directories"). CIP-57 has no Specification-versioning section today, and this change is purely additive — it does not introduce a Specification version concept or alter any existing schema.

The `Discussions:` list is updated to add [aiken-lang/aiken#1270](https://github.com/aiken-lang/aiken/issues/1270) — the upstream implementor discussion that motivated this change — alongside the existing aiken-lang/aiken#972 link. Editors who prefer the meta-PR (#1203) to also be appended per CIP-1 § Header Preamble ("must include a link to the pull request that created the CIP and any pull request that modifies it"), please say so and I'll add it.

## Implementors list change

Added `Bloxbean cardano-client-lib` (https://github.com/bloxbean/cardano-client-lib) to the Implementors list — it's been a blueprint consumer for ~2 years, just wasn't listed previously.

## Open questions for reviewers

- **Consistency with existing producer output**: the new section is intended to match what current major producers already emit. Producer maintainers — please confirm (or flag divergence in) the angle-bracket grammar described here for your toolchain.
- **Tuple syntax**: the `Tuple<<A,B>>` (doubled angle bracket) convention is chosen to disambiguate from a single-argument `Tuple<A>`. If reviewers prefer the cleaner `Tuple<A,B>` and accept the ambiguity-with-single-arg edge case, happy to adjust.
- **`title` for parametric types**: should we go further and drop normative content on `title` entirely, leaving only "it's a human-readable hint"? Current draft says SHOULD prefer the unparameterized form to make it useful for code generation, but tolerates the parameterized form. Editor preference welcome.

This PR proposes a new CIP specifying the schema, algorithm registries, canonical-CBOR encoding rules, and verification procedure for a **Proof of Existence (PoE)** record carried in Cardano transaction metadata under **metadata label 309**.

### Summary

A PoE record commits one or more cryptographic content hashes to the chain; the block time of the transaction is the authoritative witness that the content existed no later than that moment. A conformant verifier needs only the transaction metadata, optionally the content bytes, and a public blockchain explorer, with no issuer server, certificate authority, or trusted intermediary at any step. The record is content-first, issuer-agnostic, storage-agnostic, standalone-verifiable, and algorithm-agile (including a registered post-quantum hybrid KEM for the optional sealed-PoE key path).

### On the CIP number

This proposal makes no claim to a CIP number; the editors assign the number and Category at triage. The `309` in this document is the CIP-10 metadata label (`transaction_metadatum_label`), which is the on-chain identifier that implementations cite, not a proposed CIP number. The folder is named `CIP-0190`.

### Relationship to CIP-10

Metadata **label 309** is already reserved as `"Proof of Existence record"` in the [CIP-10 registry](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/blob/master/CIP-0010/registry.json), and this CIP formalizes its schema. Once a CIP number is assigned, I'll add a `CIP-0010/registry.json` change to this same PR to attribute that entry and cross-link it to the number.

### Contents of this folder

- `README.md`: the proposal (drafted against the CIP-0001 template; `Status: Proposed`, `Category: Metadata`).
- `label-309.cddl`: the normative CDDL grammar for the record body.

The inline registry and error-code tables in the proposal are complete and normative. The wider machine-readable corpus, meaning the full algorithm registries, JSON Schemas, and pinned conformance vectors, lives in the public reference repository ([cardanowall/label-309](https://github.com/cardanowall/label-309)) and is linked from the proposal rather than duplicated here, to keep the folder lean.

### Reference implementations

Byte-parity reference implementations against shared canonical-CBOR test vectors are published open-source:

- TypeScript: https://github.com/cardanowall/label-309-ts
- Python: https://github.com/cardanowall/label-309-py
- Rust: https://github.com/cardanowall/label-309-rs
- CLI: https://github.com/cardanowall/label-309-cli

Feedback from the editors and community is very welcome.

This CIP describes the Ekklesia Voting Protocol: A Hydra-Powered voting and polling system leveraging CIP-67 tokens for ballot and result discovery as well as cryptographic proofs and auditability.

The CIP defines two new tokens under the CIP-67 schema: 600 + 601

- 600 Token: Defines and anchors the ballot definition to the L1 via token + inline datum. This provides an on-chain record of what was voted on. I have attempted to keep the standard at least spiritually aligned with CIP-179 | On-Chain Polling to attempt to promote tool reusability instead of needing to create entirely new tooling.
- 601 Token: This token is minted at the same time as the 600 Ballot token and is committed into the Hydra head where votes are recorded. Once voting is concluded, a results datum is attached to the 601 token and it returns to the L1 upon head closure, containing the evidence of voting results.

The CIP further describes the datum schema and auditing format for independent validation.

Stake-weighted voting models have a structural tendency to concentrate power over time, and the standard mitigations in other ecosystems rely on identity-based mechanisms that Cardano does not use and may never adopt. This CPS opens an investigation into whether Cardano's unique governance structure offers novel mechanisms for managing DRep voting power concentration without identity.
The problem is already being observed in practice: the Nakamoto coefficient for DRep voting power has been declining, and community concern over concentration is consistently surfaced in forum polls, governance roundtables, and the Beyond Minimum Viable Governance project's community research (2025–2026).
This CPS is connected to but distinct from CPS-020 (DRep incentives). The two efforts must be coordinated so that incentive design does not work against concentration mitigation, or vice versa.

This PR looks to remove the utxo input requirement from sub-txs to enable using sub-txs for pay-per-use message passing.

Consider an oracle which wants to broadcast a price of 1 ADA/DJED which should be valid for 5 minutes. Today, they either:
- **Post it on-chain as a UTxO:** This ties updates to blockchain throughput and also makes it hard to monetize the service since referencing a UTxO can be done for free.
- **Pass around a redeemer with the price:** This enables faster updates but now payments and witness verification must happen during plutus execution which is extremely resource limited.

The sub-tx makes for the perfect abstraction of a pay-per-use message because it can tie use of a redeemer to a payment and rely on the ledger to efficiently check the witness and payment. The plutus runtime can be focused exclusively on the message.

But the way CIP-118 is currently designed prevents this. Currently, all sub-txs must be unique which means using a message is first-come-first-serve. *That completely kills this entire category of use cases.*

In order for this to work, sub-txs must be replayable which can be achieved by dropping the utxo input requirement for individual sub-txs. **But this has serious risks since it means a sub-tx could be replayed forever if no cancellation rules are included.** I don't believe this is any different than using an always succeeding plutus script so my stance is that this is not the responsibility of the ledger.

If pay-per-use message passing is indeed useful, then we need to drop this ledger requirement for sub-txs. We should not drop the utxo input requirement for the overall transaction because it is needed for other reasons!

It may not be too late to update the ledger rules before the Dijkstra hardfork, but the community needs to start considering it now.

---

This CIP is a simplification of the earlier CIP draft, [Variable Deposits as Pledge](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/pull/1204) that was closed.  The intent of this CIP is to simply add DRep pledge as a ledger field in a way that mirrors pool pledge as much as reasonably possible.

Adding this CIP and then using it for anything incentives-related will likely require two hard forks.  The first to create the mechanism for DReps to add pledge and then allow for explorers, indexers, and governance tools time to catch up.  The second hard fork would be for any use case that actually uses pledge, which is left out of scope for this CIP.

One lingering question that I left out of the CIP is that pool pledge is enforced via the Mark, Set, Go snapshots, which doesn't exist for DReps.  It may be necessary to add some sort of bonding period where DReps have to meet their pledge for X amount of time before anything takes effect.  Otherwise DReps can simply add pledge, vote, and then remove it to game the system.  It's possible that such a bonding period could be defined in this CIP, but IMHO it is likely better defined in the second part.  In any case, I think it is worthy of discussion.

Metadata label 309 is already reserved in this registry as "Proof of Existence record", but the entry does not name the specification that defines it. This PR adds that pointer.

Label 309 is specified by [CIP-0190](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/tree/master/CIP-0190) (Proof of Existence Transaction Metadata), merged into this repository. The registry schema has no `url` or owner field, so the attribution belongs in the description text, the same way labels 721, 777, 867 and 3692 name CIP-0025, CIP-0027, CIP-0088 and CIP-0149 respectively.

The change is one line:

```diff
   {
     "transaction_metadatum_label": 309,
-    "description": "Proof of Existence record"
+    "description": "CIP-0190 - Proof of Existence record"
   },
```

No other entry is touched, the entry count stays at 47, and `registry.json` still validates against `registry.schema.json`. The new description is 36 characters, well inside the 256 limit.

Nothing changes on-chain. The load-bearing identifier is the integer 309; the description is human-readable documentation for wallets, explorers and indexers, which is exactly the audience that currently has no path from the label to the spec.

BROCK Bot is a Discord moderation bot. Servers pay for it in Cardano stablecoins (USDA, USDM, USDCx, DJED), and label 6607 records which Discord server a payment is for - otherwise a plain transfer to our address gives no way to tell.

Payload is one object with two keys:
`{ "6607": { "server_id": "837215135999197246", "months": 2 } }`

`server_id` is the Discord guild ID; `months` is how many 30-day increments were purchased (1–12).

It's posted only when someone buys or tops up a subscription from our payment page - one transaction per payment, signed by the user in their own wallet. Nothing automated, nothing periodic, no other bot activity touches the chain. The bot then reads the transaction back and verifies the recipient and amount itself before crediting the server; the metadata is just the reference.

This CIP is an idea taken straight out of the [Shelley Ledger Spec, Appendix C](https://github.com/intersectmbo/cardano-ledger/releases/latest/download/shelley-delegation.pdf) (ed: page 51) with minimal changes.  It is recommended to read that short section in its entirety to understand the context of the problem this CIP aims to solve.

In short, we estimate roughly 43 blocks per epoch are missed and 41.88M worth of pool stake will always vote implicit NO on relevant governance actions due to abandoned pools.  This CIP mitigates that using a similar mechanism to what is described in the ledger spec, but instead of gating by a pool stake threshold (which is harder to implement) it simply allows any non-abandoned pool to bypass pruning by submitting a pool registration update.

This PR proposes a new **Ledger**-category CIP introducing **native confidential transfers**: transaction amounts (ADA and native-token quantities) hidden on chain as additively — partially — homomorphic Pedersen commitments, verified by zero-knowledge proofs of range and per-asset value conservation. The ledger never decrypts anything; validators check proofs only.

**Motivation.** Some entities need to transact **without the rest of the world learning the details of their financial activity — above all, how much they transact and hold**. Businesses running payroll, paying suppliers, settling invoices, or managing treasuries (and individuals alike) cannot reasonably do so on a ledger where every amount is public — yet they still need a verifiable, non-custodial ledger and the ability to satisfy auditors and tax authorities. This proposal therefore aims for **confidentiality from the general public, not from oversight**: amounts are hidden from everyone except the parties the account owner deliberately authorises. The owner can, of their own volition, designate **one or more auditors** — a tax authority, an accountant, tax-reporting software — by sharing the account's single viewing key (one key per stake address). Disclosure grants read-only access, never spend authority.

**Pure privacy / anonymity transfers are explicitly out of scope.** Designs that hide identities or break the transaction graph (mixers, shielded pools, and similar) address a different need and are better served by other CIPs or solutions. This proposal targets use cases where confidentiality and auditability must coexist.

**Highlights**

- Purely **native** (ledger-level): no smart contracts, escrow, or mixer — and the Rationale now argues the native-vs-application-layer choice explicitly rather than asserting it.
- Minimal primitive set, **no trusted setup**, and **no SNARKs, pairings, or circuits**: ristretto255 (prime-order group), Pedersen commitments, aggregated Bulletproofs range proofs, Diffie–Hellman amount transport, per-asset Schnorr balancing signatures, Fiat–Shamir with namespaced domain-separation tags.
- **Partially homomorphic by design (PHE class, addition only) — deliberately *not* fully homomorphic encryption (FHE)**: balance accounting needs nothing beyond addition, subtraction, and range checks, which keeps every ledger operation at microsecond scale.
- Addresses, the transaction graph, fees, and asset identities stay **public**; only quantities are hidden. Receiving is **opt-in per account, enforced by consensus**: a viewing-key **registration certificate** (with a refundable `viewingKeyDeposit`) binds the account's `P_view` to its stake credential; key-hash and **script-hash credentials register identically — multisig/timelock treasuries are first-class citizens** of v1.
- **Bidirectional auditability from a single key, at zero extra bytes on chain**: incoming amounts by direct decryption; outgoing amounts via deterministic ephemeral scalars, recomputable from the sender's viewing key against the public registry (a structural dividend of keeping addresses public — recipient-hiding designs must pay an extra encrypted record per output for the same property).
- On-chain structures are **versioned the ledger's way** (tagged unions + numbered map keys, no in-band version fields), with a normative **guarantees-to-future-proposals** section fixing what companion CIPs may rely on, and named verification-budget protocol parameters (`maxConfidentialCommitmentsPerTx` / `PerBlock`, `viewingKeyDeposit`).
- Confidential ADA does not contribute to stake, rewards, or governance voting power while hidden; unshielding restores participation. Trade-offs documented honestly, including ~3–5× transaction size (and fees), ~10–20× verification CPU, the smart-contract exclusion while hidden, and no post-quantum security.
- Worked example, illustrative CDDL (aggregated as a draft schema in `cddl/`), and a companion **[extensions.md](https://github.com/matiwinnetou/CIPs/blob/confidential-transfers/CIP-confidential-transfers/extensions.md)** scoring 12 anticipated extensions by the problem each solves, implementation effort, impact, new-cryptography burden, and compliance posture.

**Feedback especially welcome on:**

- the proposed **CIP-1852 role `6`** derivation path for viewing keys (pending wallet-ecosystem confirmation);
- the **scope of the initial hard fork** — which low-effort extensions should be merged into this CIP or activated alongside it (viewing-key **rotation** is the lead candidate; see extensions.md);
- confirmation of the balancing-proof form (per-asset Schnorr excess, constrained to remain aggregatable);
- Plutus script addresses (deferred by design; validation rule 10).
